articles.title: STUDIO HERRSTRÖM rebrands Sony Music imprint Milkshake
articles.description: Studio Herrström's identity for Sony Music imprint Milkshake combines references from car culture, flavored drinks, and pop music into a single energetic visual language. The original splash mark has been redrawn as a rounded emblem inspired by fluid, metal, and reflections, accompanied by neon pinks, high-vis yellows, asphalt blacks, soft lilacs, and the neo-grotesque Gates typeface. Information layouts borrow from car window permits and milk carton nutrition tables, creating structured containers for track titles, release dates, copyright information, and other details across digital and promotional materials.
articles.one-liner: Studio Herrström rebranded the Sony Music imprint Milkshake, blending car culture aesthetics with carton-style typography and an energetic neon-and-asphalt color palette.

summary.what: The identity features a redrawn metallic emblem and layouts inspired by automotive window permits and nutrition labels, using the Gates typeface to structure track and release metadata.

articles.decoder: * **Neo-grotesque**: A style of sans-serif typeface characterized by relatively high legibility and a neutral, functional appearance.

articles.title: Fit height to background pattern size with calc-size()
articles.description: CSS background patterns can end awkwardly when a container's content produces a height that isn't an exact multiple of the background tile, while `background-repeat: round` fixes the edge by distorting the pattern itself. Combining `calc-size()` with `round()` instead lets the browser calculate the element's natural height and round it up to the nearest multiple of the tile height. The result behaves similarly to `min-height`, preserving both the content-driven size and the original pattern proportions, though browser support remains limited.
articles.one-liner: Developers can use the experimental `calc-size()` and `round()` CSS functions to align container heights to background pattern tiles without distorting the pattern.

summary.what: Ahmad Shadeed demonstrates how `height: calc-size(auto, round(up, size, var(--tile-height)))` forces a container to snap to a multiple of its background tile height, preventing awkward pattern cut-offs.
summary.why: This approach replaces the older `background-repeat: round` hack, which forces patterns to distort/shrink to fit, by instead resizing the element container itself.
summary.takeaway: If you are targeting Chromium browsers, you can use these new CSS math functions to achieve perfect background alignment at the cost of broader browser support.

articles.decoder: * **calc-size()**: A proposed CSS function that allows performing calculations on intrinsic (auto) sizes, which were previously difficult to manipulate.

articles.title: How to Turn an AI-Generated Logo into a Professional Logo
articles.description: AI-generated logos work as starting concepts, not finished brand assets, and need real editing before professional use.
articles.one-liner: AI logo generators are useful concept-starting tools, but they require significant manual vectorization, typography refinement, and testing to become viable brand assets.

summary.what: Muhammad Faisal outlines a 12-step process for converting AI-generated logos into professional identities, highlighting the need to rebuild designs in vector software like Adobe Illustrator to ensure scalability and originality.
summary.why: The article addresses the common trap of treating AI outputs as final products, which often fail due to inconsistent line weight, poor typography, and potential trademark infringement.
summary.takeaway: Before using an AI-generated logo, perform a reverse image search to check for existing similarities and manually rebuild the symbol in a vector format.

articles.decoder:
* **Raster image**: A digital image represented by a grid of pixels (e.g., PNG, JPEG) that loses quality when scaled up.
* **Vector artwork**: A digital image based on mathematical paths (e.g., SVG, AI) that can be resized indefinitely without loss of quality.
* **Favicon**: The small icon displayed in a browser tab or bookmark bar representing a website.

articles.title: How Any Designer Can Build a More Open Design Culture at Work
articles.description: Designers at any level can build a more open design culture by creating psychological safety one conversation at a time.
articles.one-liner: Designers can improve team culture by prioritizing psychological safety through small, consistent feedback loops and open communication channels.

summary.what: The article suggests that designers at any seniority level can shift organizational dynamics by actively soliciting critique and normalizing vulnerability in design reviews.
summary.why: Teams often struggle with siloed design processes where fear of criticism inhibits iteration; institutionalizing openness is a cultural intervention rather than a technical one.
summary.takeaway: In your next design critique, explicitly ask for specific negative feedback on a single component to model vulnerability for your teammates.

articles.deep-summary:
* Establish shared language for design critiques to remove personal ego.
* Conduct 'open studio' sessions where work-in-progress is shown before it is polished.
* Explicitly state that unfinished work is open for radical revision.
* Use document tools that allow for public commenting to decentralize feedback.
* Encourage non-designers to participate in early-stage brainstorming to break down department barriers.
articles.decoder: * **Psychological safety**: A work environment where team members feel safe to take risks and be vulnerable in front of each other without fear of being embarrassed or punished.
